impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method claims directed to administering a genus of anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache permits broad functional genus claims where any member of the genus would be effective for the claimed treatment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, over a dissent arguing the decision undermines enablement standards for method claims post-Amgen. The dissent contended the panel's holding sustains overly broad claims that will undermine medical innovation and is contrary to Supreme Court enablement precedent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims covering a genus of biological compounds may benefit from a more permissive enablement standard where the functional limitation (treatment efficacy) is inherently satisfied by all genus members.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors in the pharmaceutical and biologics space face broader patent exclusivity, potentially blocking development of alternative antibodies within claimed genera and increasing licensing costs.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages models and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a dispute over automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's award, while affirming liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from broader acceptance of damages models in trade secret cases and stronger protection for jury awards on contract damages, reinforcing the value of proprietary technology in licensing relationships.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk and potentially larger damages exposure on remand.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive licensee that shifted its business to patent enforcement had 'ceased business operations' triggering automatic termination of the license, and whether the license conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient to sue without joining the patent owner.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's shift to enforcement activities did not constitute cessation of business operations under the license agreement with Texas A&M, and that the agreement conveyed all substantial rights in the patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue in its own name without joining the university.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees, including patent assertion entities, gain significant clarity that enforcement-focused business models do not trigger termination clauses and that broadly drafted exclusive licenses can confer standing to sue independently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a key defense strategy of challenging exclusive licensee standing, and may face more patent enforcement suits from entities whose sole business is litigation.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems satisfy the patent eligibility requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 101 under the Alice framework, and whether damages and infringement findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims relating to non-uniform constellation designs while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement, and affirmed the damages award. The decision provides important guidance on how § 101 eligibility applies to communications technology patents that optimize mathematical relationships.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications and signal processing technologies retain substantial protection where claims are tied to specific technical implementations rather than abstract mathematical concepts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry-standard communication protocols face continued patent infringement liability and damages exposure, particularly where standards incorporate patented non-uniform constellation designs.

impacts.caseName: Netlist, Inc. v. Micron Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's determination that claims of a patent directed to computer memory module architecture with data buffers were unpatentable as obvious over prior art combinations was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the PTAB's finding that all challenged claims of the '339 patent covering memory module buffer technology were obvious. The decision impacts the competitive landscape in the computer memory industry where Netlist has been actively enforcing its memory module patents against major manufacturers.
impacts.positiveImplications: Memory chip manufacturers like Micron gain freedom to operate without licensing certain memory module buffer patents, reducing costs in a high-volume commodity market.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the computer memory space face increased risk that incremental improvements to well-known memory architectures will be found obvious in IPR proceedings.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the relevant inquiry for motivation to combine prior art references in an obviousness analysis is whether the combination would be operable for the purposes of the claimed invention, rather than for the intended purpose of the individual prior art reference.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the PTAB's finding of obviousness, holding that the proper test for motivation to combine is whether the combination is operable for the purposes of the claimed invention, not whether it preserves all benefits of individual prior art references. This clarifies an important standard for obviousness analysis in IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: IPR petitioners benefit from a broader standard for establishing motivation to combine, making it easier to invalidate patents by showing combinations are operable for the claimed purpose even if key benefits of individual references are lost.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent owners face a more challenging defense against obviousness challenges, as they cannot defeat motivation to combine merely by showing the combination would undermine the purposes of individual prior art references.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement phrase 'survives the EPR,' or whether this is a state-law contract interpretation issue properly heard by the regional circuit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract dispute about whether asserted patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, finding the case turned on state-law contract interpretation rather than a substantial patent law question. The case was transferred to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlement agreements gain clarity that disputes over contractual payment triggers tied to patent office proceedings may be resolved under state contract law in regional circuits, potentially offering more favorable or predictable forums.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties may face uncertainty about which appellate court has jurisdiction over patent settlement disputes, creating forum-selection risks and potential delays from jurisdictional transfers.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even if not indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds, holding that the patent failed to enable the full scope of the claims covering impedance matching to air. This demonstrates the court's willingness to reach alternative invalidity grounds to affirm final judgments.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not relied upon below, providing additional paths to defeat patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that even if they successfully appeal one invalidity theory, courts may independently invalidate claims on other grounds raised but not decided below.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court abused its discretion in dismissing a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a patent infringement suit without leave to amend, the § 285 fee award of over $207,000 to Volkswagen, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court emphasized that the plaintiff had implicitly agreed not to amend in exchange for an extension and that the proposed amended complaint was futile.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in frivolous patent cases benefit from strong precedent supporting fee-shifting and attorney sanctions, deterring meritless patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face meaningful financial risk from aggressive enforcement of fee-shifting and sanction provisions where claims are deemed meritless or where procedural agreements are violated.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court's denial of Rule 11 sanctions and § 285 attorney fees must be supported by sufficient reasoning to permit meaningful appellate review, particularly where the patent holder had notice that related patent claims were rejected under § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's denial of sanctions and fees, remanding for the court to provide adequate reasoning. The decision arose from a case where the patentee pursued infringement claims despite PTO rejections of related claims under § 101 and a sister-court invalidation of a related patent, raising questions about litigation misconduct.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in patent cases obtain stronger procedural protections requiring courts to adequately explain denials of fee and sanction motions, enabling more effective appellate review of potential litigation abuse.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs face greater scrutiny when pursuing infringement claims where related patents or applications have been rejected or invalidated on eligibility grounds, increasing the risk of exceptional case findings.

impacts.caseName: Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's use of the invoice date as the 'date of sale' under 19 C.F.R. § 351.401(i) for calculating antidumping duty rates on Turkish steel rebar imports was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed Commerce's use of Kaptan's invoice date rather than an alternative date as the date of sale for antidumping duty calculations on Turkish rebar imports. The decision reinforces Commerce's regulatory presumption favoring invoice dates and its broad discretion in antidumping proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and trade coalitions benefit from the court's deference to Commerce's established methodology, maintaining protection against dumped imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign exporters face continued difficulty in challenging Commerce's date-of-sale determinations, which can significantly affect calculated dumping margins and resulting duty rates.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court's construction of 'internal diameter' in a patent claim directed to oil and gas wellbore float tools was correct, and whether the infringement and validity findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the judgment finding infringement of patents covering float tool technology used in oil and gas well casing operations, indicating errors in the claim construction that affected infringement and potentially validity determinations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas services sector benefit from more rigorous claim construction standards that may narrow the scope of competitor patents covering downhole tools.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy services industry face uncertainty from remand and potential narrowing of claim scope, affecting their ability to exclude competitors from using similar float tool designs.
